Transcript:
00:00 Ava Chen: Hey everyone, um thanks for joining. I'm Ava from Redwood, AE on the account. Marcus is our SE and we'll run through scope and milestones. Lina, Rajiv, Tom, thanks for setting time.
00:12 Lina Gomez: Thanks Ava. Quick note, we have 45 minutes blocked, hope that's okay. We're mostly here to nail down success criteria and what you need from us to get started.
00:22 Marcus Patel: Yep, quick agenda—confirm success metrics, traffic & dataset, security/access, test plan, and timeline. We'll read out a milestone calendar.
00:32 Rajiv Menon: Perfect. On our side the primary goal is to demonstrate 95th p50 latency under load and match current quality on rerank, and show predictable unit cost. So cost per 1k queries is a big one.
00:46 Ava Chen: Great, so success criteria draft—(1) latency SLO: 95th <= 220ms for the short ctx path, (2) quality: NDCG@10 within 1% of baseline or better on our eval set, (3) cost: per-query token-cost within 30% of their current infra, and (4) reliability: no more than two errors per 10k requests during tests. Does that align?
01:12 Lina Gomez: Yes, that maps. One ask—can you also include an availability metric we can show to execs? Uptime during test windows ideally > 99.5%.
01:26 Marcus Patel: We can add that. For benchmarks we'll run a few profiles: steady-state qps, burst tests to emulate flash traffic, and an end-to-end rerank pipeline that includes embedding + rerank calls.
01:40 Tom Baxter: Our steady-state is about 120 qps for the search front-end, but the reranker is 30 qps. Peak bursts hit 450 qps for a few minutes during business hours.
01:55 Rajiv Menon: Also average payload size is about 2.2k tokens per request once you include context. Some of that is cached prefix content.
02:06 Marcus Patel: Good detail—helps pick batching and model size. For the POC we typically test two model variants: a smaller quantized model for cost-friendly path and a full 8-bit/16-bit model for quality path. We'll propose specific families after we see sample payloads.
02:26 Lina Gomez: Timeline question—how long until you need access to our VPC and sample data?
02:32 Ava Chen: Ideally week 1. We have an access checklist—VPC peering or private link, S3 read role for sample data, KMS access for any encrypted buckets. We also can run through a hosted route if you prefer to avoid network setup for the first run.
02:50 Tom Baxter: We'd prefer VPC peering but need to run it through our infra team. We'll aim to open the ticket today. What's the security review required?
03:00 Marcus Patel: For Private deployments we ask for SOC2 attestation and our standard network diagram. We can also run under Redwood Dedicated for isolated capacity; the data never leaves your region. I'll email the security pack right after.
03:18 Lina Gomez: Good. On data residency, we need logs to be retained in-region and KMS keys customer-managed.
03:26 Ava Chen: Noted. That will be in the runbook.
03:30 (crosstalk)
03:34 Rajiv Menon: Back to benchmarks—what's the expected turnaround from you on initial perf numbers once you have access?
03:40 Marcus Patel: Typical pattern: access + sample data -> 48-72 hours for first smoke perf run -> 1 week for deeper steady-state profiling and cost analysis. So we'd expect an initial report within 3 days of access and a full dump within 7 business days.
03:58 Lina Gomez: That fits our internal schedule. Next, can you outline the mid-point review? What do we bring to that meeting?
04:06 Ava Chen: Mid-point review (week 4) should include: results to date (latency/cost/quality), ops observations (error types, tail latency causes), recommended config (batching, cache keys, quantization), and a narrow plan for the exec readout. We'll ask you to bring a couple of executive slides and the baseline metrics to compare.
04:28 Tom Baxter: For the exec readout, what do you usually present?
04:32 Marcus Patel: We present a short deck: POC goals, baseline vs POC numbers, cost delta, risk/mitigation, and recommended production rollout (dedicated/dedicated with burst, or private). It's usually 20 minutes.
04:45 Rajiv Menon: Regarding tooling, we want token-level cost traces and a breakdown per route. Is that available in the POC?
04:53 Ava Chen: Yes, Redwood Console will show token-level cost and per-route latency. For POC we'll give a short retention snapshot and a sample dashboard.
05:01 Lina Gomez: Ok good. Anything else on acceptance criteria?
05:04 Rajiv Menon: One more—quality guardrails: we want a small matrix of prompt / rerank testcases and a fail threshold. If any of the 10 core queries fall below 0.98 of baseline, we label as quality-regression.
05:20 Marcus Patel: We'll codify that as part of the eval harness. We'll push the harness and instructions to your S3 in the runbook.
05:27 (brief pause)
05:33 Ava Chen: Logistics—milestones recap: 
- Today: kickoff (this call)
- By 2025-04-18: Redwood sends runbook and initial model proposals
- By 2025-04-21: Arcadia provides sample payloads, S3 access, VPC peering details
- Week of 2025-04-28: initial perf smoke tests complete
- Week of 2025-05-12: mid-point review (detailed steady-state results)
- Week of 2025-05-26: exec readout (tentative)
06:00 Lina Gomez: That calendar works for our execs as long as the mid-point review is in the second week of May.
06:06 Tom Baxter: On VPC peering, we'll need CIDRs and a public key for the peering—Marcus, what's the minimal info you need?
06:15 Marcus Patel: At minimum: your VPC CIDRs, allowed ports (443 inbound for private link, and a small range for admin SSH if you want to keep a bastion), and an S3 role ARN we can assume for read. We'll create a short template.
06:28 Rajiv Menon: A question on model hosting: can you do A/B between hosted and dedicated during POC? We'd like to see a hosted baseline vs dedicated perf.
06:36 Marcus Patel: Yes—we can route a percentage of traffic to Redwood Hosted API and the remainder to a Redwood Dedicated instance in your region. It helps show cost/latency tradeoffs. Note: hosted introduces egress across region boundaries sometimes; we'll call that out.
06:52 Lina Gomez: Any compliance red flags for us to be worried about during POC?
06:56 Marcus Patel: No, we run under our SOC2. For additional requirements (HIPAA, PCI) we can sign a DPA and add controls; that'll likely push timelines by 1-2 weeks.
07:10 Tom Baxter: We're not HIPAA. We'll stick with SOC2 and KMS integration.
07:15 Ava Chen: Great. On benchmarks—specific metrics we will deliver back: p50/p95 latency, p99 if possible, error rate, throughput, tokens per request, cost per 1k queries, NDCG, and a short per-route cost waterfall.
07:34 Rajiv Menon: For the rerank pipeline we have a 2-step call: embedding generation then reranker inference. We want combined E2E numbers and component-level numbers.
07:44 Marcus Patel: We'll run both component and E2E tests. For caching scenario we'll simulate prefix cache hit rates of 40%/70%/90% to report sensitivity.
07:55 (background noise, brief)
08:00 Lina Gomez: Can you put together an explicit list of artifacts you'll produce?
08:04 Ava Chen: Sure—POC runbook, benchmark scripts, perf report (csv + slides), suggested prod config, and a short ops runbook for rollouts. We'll also share the eval harness and example dashboard links.
08:17 Tom Baxter: Good. Who owns mitigations if we see quality regressions mid-POC?
08:22 Marcus Patel: We'll triage with you. Typical mitigations: switch quantization profile, increase model size, tune batching, or route to a higher tier during spikes. We'll include fallbacks in the runbook.
08:36 Rajiv Menon: Can you estimate cost to run the POC itself? Does Redwood charge for the POC infra?
08:43 Ava Chen: Standard practice—no charge for the baseline POC if it runs within our hosted sandbox. If you require Dedicated reserved capacity for the POC we'll discuss nominal credits or a short-term invoice; we can be flexible. We'll outline options in the runbook.
08:58 Lina Gomez: Ok that helps for budgeting. On the model selection, can you give a quick rule of thumb—what families are you likely to recommend for a reranker?
09:06 Marcus Patel: For rerank we usually pick a medium transformer tuned for retrieval tasks. If latency is paramount we'll try a distilled/quantized variant; if quality is king we go with the larger 7B-13B family depending on tokens. We'll propose two concrete options after we see payloads.
09:25 (pause)
09:30 Ava Chen: Any risks we should call out now?
09:33 Tom Baxter: Network changes timeline—peering could take 3-5 business days. Internal approvals can add slack.
09:39 Rajiv Menon: Also dataset anonymization—we need to scrub PII before handing over. That could add a day or two.
09:46 Ava Chen: Good to flag. We'll mark those on the timeline and set conservative dates.
09:52 (typing)
10:00 Marcus Patel: Quick operational note: we'll need a common test account in S3 with example objects and a small replay harness. If you already use a qps simulator, we can take those logs.
10:12 Lina Gomez: We'll get you a sample 24-hour trace and a small 1k-query test set.
10:18 Ava Chen: Perfect. Let's talk about the mid-point meeting deliverables again just so it's crystal—Marcus?
10:24 Marcus Patel: Mid-point: consolidated perf metrics (CSV), annotated tail latency causes, suggested config for production, and an adjusted runbook for a 1-week pilot. We'll demo the console and dashboards for token-level cost.
10:38 Lina Gomez: That sounds good. One last question—how do we measure 'predictable unit cost'? Do you provide a cost-per-token simulation?
10:47 Marcus Patel: Yes, we produce per-route cost simulation based on observed tokens and throughput. We'll show both raw and amortized costs with caching factored in.
10:55 Rajiv Menon: Great. Any other blockers?
10:58 Tom Baxter: I'll open the infra ticket today, Rajiv will scrub the sample dataset and drop in S3, and Lina will coordinate exec availability.

11:16 Lina Gomez: Please tentatively put it the week of 2025-05-12 and we'll confirm after the smoke run.
